intro: Buddhists tell hundreds of stories about the Buddha's lives before he was the Buddha. These are called Jataka tales. In many of them, he is an animal.
In this unit you will hear two of them. A Monkey King saves his friends. A hare gives the only gift he has. You will be able to retell each tale and say what it teaches.
bigQuestion: What can animal stories teach about kindness and giving?

timeline.t: Monkeys live happily in a mango tree by a river.
A human king and his archers circle the tree.
The Monkey King makes a bridge with his body.
The monkeys cross, and the human king learns about good leaders.
Four friends decide to give gifts to anyone in need.
A hungry traveler comes, and three friends find food.
The hare offers himself, and the fire feels cool.
The tale says Sakka draws the hare on the moon.

write.prompt: Pick the Monkey King or the hare. Tell what the animal did and why. Name the tale and what Buddhists say it teaches.
tips: Name the tale, like "the Hare Jataka."
Use one word from the unit, like courage or share.

title: Jataka Tales

chapters.title: The Monkey King's Bridge
chapters.bigQuestion: What does the Monkey King's story teach about being a good leader?

story.title: Across the Monkey King's Back
story.kicker: Eighty thousand monkeys need a way across the river.
paragraphs: Buddhists tell this old tale. By a wide river stood a mango tree. Its mangoes were big and sweet. A Monkey King and eighty thousand monkeys lived in it.
One night a human king came with archers. They wanted the mangoes. They circled the tree. The monkeys shook with fear. "We are trapped!" they cried.
The Monkey King had a plan. He tied a long vine to his foot. He leaped across the river and tied the vine to a tree. But the vine was too short.
So he held a branch with his hands. His own body became the last part of the bridge. One by one, the monkeys ran across his back to safety.
story.think: Why do you think the Monkey King used his own body?

lessons.title: Stories of Earlier Lives
lessons.mainIdea: Jataka tales are stories Buddhists tell about the Buddha's earlier lives.
reading: Buddhists believe that people are born many times. They tell stories about the Buddha's lives before he was the Buddha. These are called Jataka tales.
There are over 500 Jataka tales. In many of them, the Buddha-to-be is an animal. He might be a monkey, a deer or a hare.

words.d: a story Buddhists tell about one of the Buddha's earlier lives

lessons.title: Why Tell Them?
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists use Jataka tales to teach kindness, courage and wisdom.
reading: Jataka tales are told to children and grown-ups. Teachers tell them at temples. Parents tell them at home.
Each tale shows a good way to act. Buddhists say they teach kindness, courage and wisdom. Many are painted on temple walls in Asia.

words.d: being brave when something is hard

look.title: A Painted Wall
look.text: Look at a temple wall covered with paintings. Here is a monkey. There is a deer. A hare sits by a fire. Each picture tells a story.
look.prompt: Why might a temple paint stories on its walls?

check.why: Buddhists use the tales to teach good ways to act.

choices: being brave when things are hard
check.why: Courage means being brave when something is hard.
Many temples in Asia have Jataka paintings on their walls.

lessons.title: A Living Bridge
lessons.mainIdea: The Monkey King made his body into a bridge to save his monkeys.
reading: This tale is called the Great Monkey King. It is Jataka number 407. The Monkey King saw his monkeys were in danger.
He stretched his body across the river. The monkeys ran over his back. It hurt him, but he kept holding on. All of his monkeys got away.

look.title: The Monkey King's Choice
look.text: The Monkey King held on to the tree while all his monkeys crossed over his back. He was hurt, but he was glad they were safe.
look.cite: Jataka no. 407, Mahakapi Jataka (the Great Monkey King), retold from The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, vol. 3 (1897)
look.prompt: How did the Monkey King feel when his monkeys were safe?

check.q: What did the Monkey King make?
check.why: He stretched his body to finish the bridge.
The archers were coming, and he wanted his monkeys safe.

check.q: What is the name of this tale?
check.why: It is the Mahakapi Jataka, the Great Monkey King.

lessons.title: The Human King Learns
lessons.mainIdea: The human king watched and learned what a good leader does.
reading: The human king saw everything. He saw the Monkey King get hurt to save the others. He was amazed.
The king had the Monkey King gently cared for. The tale says the Monkey King told him a good leader cares for the ones he leads. The king listened.

words.d: a person who helps and guides a group

look.title: Two Kings
look.text: One king came to take mangoes. One king gave his own body to help others. At the end, the first king learned from the second.
look.prompt: What did the human king learn?

check.why: The human king saw the whole brave act.

check.q: What does a good leader do, says the tale?
check.why: The Monkey King says a good leader cares for those he leads.
A leader helps and guides a group.

lessons.title: Tales Like These
lessons.mainIdea: Many cultures tell animal stories that teach a lesson.
reading: People everywhere tell animal stories. The Aesop fables come from Greece. The Panchatantra comes from India. They teach lessons too.
The Jatakas are special to Buddhists. They are about the Buddha's earlier lives. Buddhists say he grew kinder and wiser in each life.

words.d: a short animal story that teaches a lesson

look.title: Two Animal Stories
look.text: In Aesop, a slow tortoise wins a race against a fast hare. In a Jataka, a Monkey King saves his friends. Both stories use animals to teach.
look.prompt: What lesson does each story teach?

check.q: Where do Aesop's fables come from?
check.why: Aesop's fables come from ancient Greece.

check.q: What makes Jatakas special to Buddhists?
choices: they tell the Buddha's earlier lives
check.why: Buddhists tell Jatakas as the Buddha's earlier lives.

choices: a short animal story with a lesson
check.why: A fable is a short animal story that teaches a lesson.

lessons.title: Kindness and Courage in Class
lessons.mainIdea: The Jataka values of kindness and courage can be seen in everyday life.
reading: The Monkey King was brave and kind. You do not need to be a king to help. Holding a door is kind. Helping a friend who fell is kind.
Being brave can be small too. You can try something new. You can say, "Can I help?" Small acts can help a whole group.

words.d: being caring and helpful to others

look.title: A Helper at Recess
look.text: Look at the playground. A small boy drops his ball near the fence. A girl runs over. She picks it up and hands it back with a smile.
look.prompt: How is the girl like the Monkey King?

check.why: Helping someone who fell shows kindness, like the Monkey King.
Trying something new or offering help can take courage.
Kindness means being caring and helpful to others.

chapters.title: The Hare in the Moon
chapters.bigQuestion: What does the hare's gift teach about giving what you can?

story.title: Four Friends and a Gift
story.kicker: The hare comes back with nothing but an idea.
paragraphs: Buddhists tell this Jataka tale. Four friends lived by a forest. They were a hare, a monkey, a jackal and an otter. They wanted to give a gift to anyone in need.
One day a hungry traveler came by. The otter found fish. The jackal found some food. The monkey picked mangoes. Each friend had something to give.
The hare only ate grass. People cannot eat grass. The hare thought and thought. Then he had an idea. "I will give myself," he said.
The traveler made a fire. The hare jumped in. But the fire felt cool as snow! The traveler was really Sakka, a king of the gods in the story. He was testing the friends.
story.think: Why was the hare's gift so surprising?

lessons.title: Hare, Monkey, Jackal, Otter
lessons.mainIdea: Four animal friends in the Hare Jataka each wanted to give a gift.
reading: This tale is called the Hare Jataka. It is Jataka number 316. Buddhists tell that the wise hare was the Buddha in an earlier life.
The hare had three friends. They were a monkey, a jackal and an otter. The hare taught them to be kind and to share.

words.d: an animal like a big rabbit with long ears
a furry animal that swims and catches fish

look.title: What Each Friend Found
rows: friends who found food for a person
look.cite: Jataka no. 316, Sasa Jataka, in The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, vol. 3 (1897)
look.prompt: How many friends found food a person could eat?

check.why: The Hare Jataka tells of a hare, a monkey, a jackal and an otter.

check.q: Who was the Buddha-to-be in this tale?
check.why: Buddhists tell that the wise hare was the Buddha in an earlier life.
An otter is a furry animal that swims and catches fish.

lessons.title: Finding Gifts
lessons.mainIdea: Each friend found food to share, except the hare.
reading: The otter found fish in the river. The jackal found some food. The monkey picked sweet mangoes from a tree.
The hare looked around. He only had grass. He knew a person could not eat grass. What could he give?

words.d: to give some of what you have to others

look.title: Only Grass
look.text: Look at the hare in the field. His friends run past carrying fish and fruit. He sits in the green grass. His ears go up. He is thinking hard.
look.prompt: What do you think the hare feels?

check.why: In the tale, the monkey picked mangoes.
The hare ate grass, which a person could not eat.

choices: give some of what you have
check.why: To share means to give some of what you have to others.

lessons.title: Giving Himself
lessons.mainIdea: In the tale, the hare offered himself because he had nothing else.
reading: The hare wanted to give something. He had only himself. So he offered himself as food for the traveler.
The traveler lit a fire. The hare jumped in. But the tale says the fire did not burn him at all. It felt as cool as snow.

words.d: to hold something out for someone to take

look.title: The Fire Was Cool
look.text: The hare leaped into the fire, glad to give. But the flames did not even warm a single hair. It felt like jumping into snow.
look.cite: Jataka no. 316, Sasa Jataka, retold from The Jataka, ed. E.B. Cowell, vol. 3 (1897)
look.prompt: What surprising thing happened in the fire?

check.why: With no food to give, the hare offered himself.
The tale says the fire did not burn him and felt cool.

choices: hold out for someone to take
check.why: To offer is to hold something out for someone to take.

lessons.title: Sakka's Test
lessons.mainIdea: The traveler was Sakka, who was testing the hare's kindness.
reading: The traveler was not really a traveler. The tale says he was Sakka, a king of the gods. He came to test the four friends.
Sakka saw that the hare's kindness was real. He did not let the hare be hurt. He praised the hare's big heart.

words.d: a king of the gods in Buddhist stories

look.title: A Hidden Visitor
look.text: Many stories have a visitor in disguise. The visitor looks plain. At the end, we learn who they really are. Then we see why they came.
look.prompt: Why do you think Sakka came in disguise?

check.why: The tale says the traveler was Sakka in disguise.
Sakka came to test their kindness.
In the tale, Sakka kept the hare safe.

lessons.title: A Picture on the Moon
lessons.mainIdea: The tale says Sakka painted the hare on the moon so all would remember.
reading: Sakka wanted everyone to remember the hare's gift. The tale says he drew the shape of a hare on the moon.
Look at the full moon. Some dark spots look like a rabbit. Buddhists tell this tale to explain the picture.

words.d: the round light we see in the night sky

look.title: The Full Moon
look.text: Look at the full moon on a clear night. It is round and bright. There are gray shapes on it. Some people see a face. Some see a rabbit with long ears.
look.prompt: What shape do you see when you look at the moon?

check.q: What did Sakka draw on the moon?
check.why: The tale says Sakka drew the hare on the moon.

choices: so all would remember the gift
check.why: He wanted everyone to remember the hare's kindness.

check.q: When can you best see the rabbit shape?
check.why: The shape shows best on the bright full moon.

lessons.title: Moon Rabbits Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: People in Japan, China and other places also tell of a rabbit in the moon.
reading: In Japan and China, people also tell about a rabbit in the moon. In some stories the rabbit makes rice cakes or medicine.
Many families look at the moon at the fall moon festival. They share treats. They think about giving what you can.

words.d: a special day when people gather to celebrate

look.title: A Moon Festival
look.text: Look at a family on a porch in the fall. The moon is big and round. A grandma points up and tells about the rabbit in the moon. Everyone shares round cakes.
look.prompt: What might the family be thinking about as they look at the moon?

check.q: Where else do people tell of a moon rabbit?
check.why: Moon rabbit stories are told in Japan, China and other places.

check.q: What does the rabbit make in some stories?
check.why: In some Japanese and Chinese stories the rabbit makes rice cakes or medicine.
A festival is a special day when people gather to celebrate.
